content: 1. A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted to evaluate interventions in the workplace aimed at addressing depressive symptoms. This study was published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine. 2. Stubbs et al. provided guidance from the European Psychiatric Association (EPA) on the use of physical activity as a treatment for severe mental illness. This meta-review of evidence was supported by the International Organization of Physical Therapists in Mental Health and published in European Psychiatry in 2018. 3. De Oliveira et al. performed an economic analysis of workplace interventions targeting mental health and substance use. Their systematic literature review and narrative synthesis were published in The Lancet Psychiatry in 2020. 4. Nieuwenhuijsen et al. reviewed interventions designed to improve return-to-work outcomes for individuals with depression. This Cochrane systematic review was published in 2020. 5. Arends et al. examined interventions aimed at facilitating the return to work for adults diagnosed with adjustment disorders. Their findings were published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in 2012. 6. A publication titled Sick on the Job? Myths and Realities about Mental Health and Work explored the relationship between mental health and workplace dynamics, addressing common misconceptions. 7. Da Silva Junior and Fischer analyzed disability claims due to mental illness in Brazil between 2008 and 2011, focusing on social security benefits. Their findings were published in the Revista de Saúde Pública in 2014. 8. Corbière et al. conducted a scoping review to identify the roles and actions of stakeholders in the return-to-work process for employees on sick leave due to common mental disorders. This study was published in the Journal of Occupational Rehabilitation in 2020. 9. Rebergen et al. evaluated the cost-effectiveness of guideline-based care for workers experiencing mental health issues. Their research was published in the Journal of Occupational and Environmental Medicine in 2009. 10. Lokman et al. compared return-to-work interventions with usual care for employees on sick leave. Their health-economic appraisal, conducted alongside a cluster randomized trial, was published in BMJ Open in 2017. 11. Taimela et al. assessed the cost-effectiveness of an occupational health intervention program for workers at high risk of sickness absence. This analysis, based on a randomized controlled trial, was published in Occupational and Environmental Medicine in 2008. 12. Suijkerbuijk et al. conducted a network meta-analysis of interventions aimed at obtaining and maintaining employment for adults with severe mental illness. Their findings were published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in 2017. 13. Kinoshita et al. reviewed the effectiveness of supported employment programs for adults with severe mental illness. This Cochrane systematic review was published in 2013. 14. Van Rijn et al. evaluated the effectiveness of re-employment programs for unemployed individuals with severe mental health problems, focusing on health and quality of life outcomes. Their systematic review and meta-analysis were published in 2016. 15. Fadyl et al. assessed the effectiveness of vocational interventions in helping individuals with mild to moderate mental health conditions secure paid employment. Their systematic review and meta-analysis were published in BMJ Open in 2020. 16. Marshall et al. investigated factors associated with under-reporting of mental health symptoms among police officers during mental health screening. Their study was published in BMC Psychiatry in 2021. 17. Technical and ethical guidelines for workers' health surveillance were developed to ensure effective monitoring and support for occupational health. 18. The International Labour Organization (ILO) provided recommendations on occupational health services, emphasizing the importance of training and regular participation in occupational safety and health initiatives. 19. Screening programs were designed to enhance effectiveness, maximize benefits, and minimize harm, as outlined in a short guide by the World Health Organization (WHO). 20. Ethical considerations in workplace governance were addressed in the Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct, emphasizing the importance of integrity and professionalism. 21. Shea et al. introduced AMSTAR 2, a critical appraisal tool for systematic reviews that include randomized or non-randomized studies of healthcare interventions. This tool was published in BMJ in 2017. 22. Guyatt et al. described the GRADE system, which provides a framework for rating the quality of evidence and the strength of recommendations in clinical and public health guidelines. This was published in BMJ in 2008. 23. Hultcrantz et al. clarified the concept of certainty of evidence within the GRADE framework, as published in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology in 2017. 24. Rehfuess et al. discussed integrating WHO norms and values with a complexity perspective in global health decision-making. This was published in BMJ Global Health in 2019. 25. Alonso-Coello et al. introduced the GRADE Evidence to Decision (EtD) frameworks, which offer a systematic and transparent approach to making informed healthcare decisions. This was published in BMJ in 2016. 26. Guyatt et al. outlined the process of translating evidence into actionable recommendations, as published in BMJ in 2008. 27. The WHO guidelines on mental health at work emphasized the importance of addressing workplace-related mental health outcomes, including absenteeism, presenteeism, productivity, and job satisfaction. 28. Psychosocial interventions, such as cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), interpersonal therapy (IPT), and stress management techniques, were highlighted as effective strategies for improving mental health outcomes. 29. The concept of burnout was defined as a syndrome resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed, often manifesting as emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, and reduced personal accomplishment. 30. Mental health was defined as a state of well-being that enables individuals to cope with life’s stresses, realize their abilities, and contribute to their communities. It is an integral component of overall health and well-being. 31. Psychosocial disability was described as a form of disability arising from long-term mental impairments that interact with societal barriers, such as stigma and discrimination, hindering full participation in society. 32. The guidelines emphasized the importance of evidence-based psychosocial interventions, including psychoeducation, peer support, and supported employment, in improving mental health outcomes in lowand middle-income countries.
